sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
sections.body_md:
Classification is a complete pass over the stationary points, not a check of one favorite candidate. You compute the gradient, set it equal to zero, and solve the system for every real solution. Each solution then gets a Hessian test. Positive definite means a strict local minimizer. Negative definite means a strict local maximizer. Indefinite means a saddle. A zero eigenvalue means the second-order test has nothing to say, and the point has to be settled by the sign of the function or by a higher-order look.

A local label is not a global label. After the list is classified, a global claim needs an extra reason. Coercivity, or a compact sublevel set, says a global minimizer exists, and it must be one of the local minimizers you found, because every interior minimizer is stationary. Comparing the values at the local minimizers then names the global ones.

The same discipline catches a false global claim. A note that stops at the first point where the gradient vanishes has not looked at the other solutions, and it has not checked the behavior at infinity.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md: Solve \(\nabla f(x) = 0\). At each solution evaluate the eigenvalues of \(H_f\). The point is a strict local minimizer when every eigenvalue is positive, a strict local maximizer when every eigenvalue is negative, and a saddle when both signs appear. For a coercive smooth function the global minimum value is the smallest value of \(f\) on the local-minimizer list. If that list is empty, a coercive function is not what you have.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(f(x, y) = x^2 + 2y^2 - 6x + 4y + 24\). The gradient is \((2x - 6,\ 4y + 4)\), so the only stationary point is \((3, -1)\). The Hessian is diagonal with entries 2 and 4, both positive, so the point is a strict local minimizer. The function is a sum of squares plus a constant after completing the square, and it tends to infinity at infinity.

The classified height is 13. The arithmetic is \(9 + 2 - 18 - 4 + 24\). There is no second stationary point to compare, and coercivity says this local value is the global minimum. A zero eigenvalue would have blocked that sentence and forced a look at the flat direction.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Stopping after one root of the gradient equation misses a lower one. The polynomial \(t^4 - 8t^2\) has a local maximum at the origin and two global minimizers at the opposite roots, and the origin is the root most people see first. Treating a zero eigenvalue as a saddle is the other standard error. The function \(x^2 + y^4\) is stationary only at the origin, the Hessian there is singular, and the origin is a strict global minimizer because the function is nonnegative. An indefinite Hessian really is a saddle. A singular one is a question mark.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Newton's method for minimization solves the same gradient equation by linearizing it, and it can converge to a saddle as easily as to a minimizer. The classification is what says which arrival is useful. On a constraint the points you classify are stationary for a Lagrangian, and the objective gradient itself may be nonzero.
